idiom_name: Window.getWindows() registry + Stage.show/close with Scene switching
implementation_notes: JavaFX keeps the registry for you: Window.getWindows() is the observable list of every window the toolkit has created, Stage is the view whose show()/close()/toFront() are the open, switch and dispose commands, and Application.start/stop bracket the whole set. Switching inside one window is a scene or root swap (for example a BorderPane centre), where the handler role is played by the application class holding the current screen plus the model, and syncing is listener-based (ChangeListener on the model, or a property each screen binds to). Use it when the codebase is JavaFX; the toolkit's window list is authoritative, so keep your own screen map as a view of it rather than as a second source of truth.
pitfalls: Window.getWindows() lists only windows the toolkit has created and drops them on close, but your own screen map does not: purge it in Stage.setOnHidden, or a disposed screen keeps listening to the model.

Replacing a pane's content (setCenter(...)) throws the previous view away together with its scroll, focus and selection state; keep per-screen state in the screen's model, or keep both views and toggle visibility instead of recreating them.
Listeners registered on the model from a screen are strong references - the classic JavaFX leak - so a closed screen stays alive along with its entire scene graph unless it unregisters.
All scene-graph mutation must happen on the JavaFX Application Thread; model callbacks arriving on another thread need Platform.runLater().

variants.name: Swing JDesktopPane with a DesktopManager (classic MDI)
variants.idiom_name: JDesktopPane.getAllFrames + JInternalFrame children + DesktopManager lifecycle hooks
variants.implementation_notes: Swing's MDI container is the classic view handler: a JDesktopPane holds the open views as JInternalFrame children, getAllFrames() is the registry, setSelectedFrame()/activateFrame() switch, and a DesktopManager (normally DefaultDesktopManager) supplies the per-frame hooks - iconifyFrame, deiconifyFrame, activateFrame, closeFrame - that make the meta-behaviour uniform. Adding a frame to the pane registers it and dispose() removes it, so registration and disposal are one call each. Prefer this variant only in existing Swing applications: it is a legacy toolkit whose look and feel and single-EDT threading model still apply.
pitfalls: Swing is single-threaded: every registry mutation and every view touch must be marshalled with SwingUtilities.invokeLater, even when the model notifies from a worker thread.
JInternalFrame.dispose() removes the frame from the desktop but not your own listeners from the model - the classic Swing memory leak.
getAllFrames() returns a snapshot array, so a frame disposed during iteration is still in the array and its methods then fail on a disposed component.
